commission: Why is there a French debt crisis?
access_order: Listed stage1; read READ-ME.md then commission.md; viewed all four PNGs sequentially in numeric order using view_image. No other input paths accessed.
operational_issues: Initial output-writing command failed because python was unavailable; retried with python3.

chart_readings.what_happened: Spending exceeded revenue throughout 1995–2025. The deficit narrowed to 1.3% of GDP in 2000, jumped to 7.4% in 2009 and 8.9% in 2020, and remained 5.1% in 2025. Spending ended at 57.2% and revenue at 52.1%.
chart_readings.why_i_think_it_happened: The largest gap increases visually come from spending jumping while revenue shares change less. Persistent gaps seem the immediate reason debt would accumulate.
chart_readings.unclear_unsupported_or_unreadable: The chart does not identify underlying policies or economic causes. Ratios cannot distinguish increased spending in euros from falling GDP. It does not explain persistence of the recent deficit. Main labels and footer are readable.

chart_readings.what_happened: Debt rose from 60.5% of GDP in Q1 2000 to 119.0%, or €3.6 trillion, in Q2 2026. There are large upward steps around the financial crisis and Covid. A decline to 109.5% at end-2023 was followed by renewed increases.
chart_readings.why_i_think_it_happened: Highlighted crisis periods suggest shocks drove major jumps. Chart 1 makes ongoing deficits a plausible explanation for the longer rise.
chart_readings.unclear_unsupported_or_unreadable: Crisis timing does not establish mechanisms. Debt/GDP fell after 2020 despite ongoing deficits in chart 1, so GDP growth or other factors must matter but are not shown. No borrowing strain or crisis threshold appears. Text is readable.

chart_readings.what_happened: France has the highest spending, revenue and deficit shares among the displayed countries. Its 2025 deficit is 5.1% versus the EU27 average of 3.1%; spending is 57.2% versus 49.5%; revenue is 52.1% versus 46.4%.
chart_readings.why_i_think_it_happened: France collects more revenue relative to GDP, but its spending premium is larger still. This makes spending seem central to its comparatively large deficit.
chart_readings.unclear_unsupported_or_unreadable: One year does not explain why the differences arose or what levels are appropriate. Germany’s displayed spending minus revenue is 2.6 points but the deficit is labeled 2.7, presumably rounding but unexplained. The bottom axis caption overlaps the source note and impairs footer readability. Main data are clear.

chart_readings.what_happened: France spends 7.7 GDP points more than the EU27 average. Cash benefits including pensions contribute 2.9 points, public-sector pay 2.1, and in-kind benefits 1.0. Goods and services bought offset the gap by 0.7 points. Interest contributes only 0.3 points.
chart_readings.why_i_think_it_happened: The spending premium is concentrated in benefits and public payroll. This gives an accounting explanation for the high spending in chart 3.
chart_readings.unclear_unsupported_or_unreadable: Cash benefits include more than pensions; the full 2.9 points cannot be attributed to pensions. Economic categories do not explain demographics, service quality, policy choices or feasibility of reductions. Bottom axis text and source/definition line overlap, making the footer hard to read. Main bars and numbers are clear.

overall.what_happened: France has persistent deficits and debt roughly doubled relative to GDP since 2000, with major crisis-era jumps and a renewed rise after 2023. Its recent deficit is comparatively large despite high revenue.
overall.why_i_think_it_happened: The packet points toward spending persistently exceeding revenue, amplified during the financial crisis and Covid. High spending compared with the EU average is concentrated in cash benefits and public-sector pay. These are accounting contributors rather than fully established deeper causes.
overall.unclear_unsupported_or_unreadable: Debt accumulation is explained more clearly than why there is a crisis now. No market stress, financing rates, debt-service trend, political constraints or future sustainability evidence is shown. The packet does not reconcile deficits with falling debt/GDP periods or establish that current spending composition caused the historical rise. Charts 3 and 4 have overlapping footer text.
